sciNatSel: Which is the best definition of an adaptation?
An inherited trait that helps survival
A habit learned from a parent
A change made by an injury
A trait that never varies
An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to pass on their genes?
Those best suited to their environment
Those that are the largest in size
Those that live alone the longest
Those that eat the most food
Individuals best suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so their genes are passed on more often.
Darwin studied finches and tortoises on which group of islands?
The Galápagos Islands
The Hawaiian Islands
The Canary Islands
The Magdalen Islands
Darwin's observations on the Galápagos Islands helped him develop the idea of natural selection.
Which of these traits could be passed on by natural selection?
Fur colour
A scar from a fight
A trick learned at a zoo
A tail lost to a predator
Fur colour is controlled by genes, so it can be inherited, unlike injuries or learned behaviours.
Why do most populations produce more offspring than can survive?
Food and space are limited
Parents always abandon their young
Offspring never need any food
Only one offspring is ever born
Because resources are limited, not all offspring survive, so individuals compete and the best-suited ones tend to survive.
What does the phrase "survival of the fittest" mean in biology?
The best-suited organisms reproduce most
The strongest animals win every fight
The fastest runners live the longest
The biggest animals eat the most
In biology, "fit" means well suited to the environment, which leads to more surviving offspring.
A population of beetles includes green and brown beetles. Birds easily spot the green ones on brown soil. Over time, the population will become …
mostly brown
mostly green
half green, half brown
completely white
Brown beetles are better hidden, so more of them survive and reproduce, passing on brown colour.
Natural selection acts on individuals, but which one actually changes over many generations?
The population
A single individual
The weather
The predator's diet
Individuals cannot change their genes; instead the mix of traits in the population changes over generations.
What is the main source of new variation in a population?
Mutations in genes
Exercise during life
Learning from parents
Injuries from predators
Mutations create new versions of genes, which add new inherited variation to a population.
Cacti have thick, waxy stems that store water. This adaptation helps them survive in …
dry deserts
wet rainforests
freshwater ponds
snowy tundra
Storing water and reducing water loss helps cacti survive where rain is rare.
Which of these is a change in a population caused by natural selection?
More hares with thick fur after cold winters
A hare grows thick fur after moving north
A hare learns to hide under a bush
A hare loses fur after a skin injury
Natural selection changes how common an inherited trait is in a population over generations.
Snowshoe hares turn white in winter. How does this help them survive?
It hides them from predators in snow
It keeps them cooler in summer heat
It helps them find more food to eat
It makes them run much faster
White winter fur camouflages hares against snow, so predators such as lynx spot them less often.
A trait that helps an organism survive in one environment might be harmful in …
a different environment
every environment
its own environment
no environment at all
Whether a trait is helpful depends on the environment, so a trait can be useful in one place and harmful in another.
Why can't natural selection make a population change in a single generation?
Trait frequencies shift slowly over generations
Animals refuse to change their habits
Genes change only when organisms grow up
Each individual must decide to adapt
Natural selection works as helpful traits become more common, which takes many generations of reproduction.
Which scientist came up with the idea of natural selection at about the same time as Darwin?
Alfred Russel Wallace
Isaac Newton
Marie Curie
Gregor Mendel
Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea of natural selection, and he and Darwin presented their ideas together in 1858.
What is the term for an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment?
Fitness
Strength
Intelligence
Speed
In biology, fitness describes how well an organism survives and reproduces compared with others.
Which helps a polar bear survive in the Arctic?
Thick fat and dense fur
Thin skin and short fur
Bright colours and spots
Large ears that lose heat
Thick fat and dense fur keep polar bears warm in very cold conditions.
Some weeds now survive a herbicide that used to kill them. What is the best explanation?
Resistant weeds survived and reproduced
The weeds learned to avoid the spray
The herbicide made the weeds stronger
Each weed chose to become resistant
A few weeds had inherited resistance, survived the spray and passed this trait to their offspring.
Which is NOT needed for natural selection to happen?
Organisms trying to change
Variation among individuals
Traits that can be inherited
More offspring than can survive
Natural selection needs variation, inheritance and competition, but not any effort by organisms to change.
Fish in a dark cave over many generations lose working eyes. Which factor most likely allowed this?
Eyes gave no survival advantage there
Fish chose to stop using their eyes
Darkness directly erased their eyes
Predators removed the fish's eyes
In total darkness, eyes do not help survival, so fish without working eyes were not at a disadvantage.
Which word describes features that help an organism blend in with its surroundings?
Camouflage
Mimicry of sound
Migration
Hibernation
Camouflage lets an organism blend in, helping it avoid predators or sneak up on prey.
What evidence did Darwin use to support natural selection?
Variation he saw among living species
Photos of DNA from his microscope
Results from modern gene testing
Satellite images of the islands
Darwin based his ideas on careful observations of variation in living organisms and fossils, long before DNA was understood.
sciXsNatSel: Peppered moths on soot-covered trees: which moths were eaten more often by birds?
Light-coloured moths, which stood out
Dark-coloured moths, which stood out
Both colours were eaten equally
Neither colour was ever eaten
Light moths were easy to see on dark bark, so birds ate them more and dark moths became more common.
After pollution laws cleaned the trees, light peppered moths became common again. Why?
Light moths were hidden on clean bark again
Dark moths all learned to change colour
The cleaner air painted the moths white
Birds stopped eating moths completely
On clean, light bark the light moths were better camouflaged, so they survived and reproduced more.
During a drought, finches with larger, stronger beaks survived better. What is the most likely reason?
They could crack the hard seeds left
They could fly farther to find rain
Their beaks stored extra water
They could sing louder for mates
During the drought only hard seeds remained, so finches with strong beaks got more food and survived.
After the drought, what happened to the average beak size of the next generation of finches?
It became larger
It became smaller
It stayed exactly the same
It disappeared completely
The surviving large-beaked finches passed on their genes, so their offspring had larger beaks on average.
Which explanation of the giraffe's long neck matches natural selection?
Longer-necked giraffes survived and had more young
Giraffes stretched their necks and passed it on
Giraffes grew long necks because they wanted to
Each giraffe's neck grew after eating leaves
Natural selection explains change through inherited variation and differences in survival, not by stretching or wanting.
Why is the idea that giraffes stretched their necks and passed this on incorrect?
Changes made during life are not inherited
Giraffes cannot stretch their necks at all
Necks are not used to reach food
Giraffes never have any offspring
Body changes gained during a lifetime do not change genes, so they cannot be passed to offspring.
A new predator that hunts by sight arrives on an island with green and red lizards living on green plants. Which prediction best follows natural selection?
Green lizards will become more common
Red lizards will become more common
All lizards will turn blue
The number of each colour stays equal
Green lizards are camouflaged against green plants, so fewer are caught and more of them reproduce.
Some mosquitoes in an area survive a common insecticide. What explains this best?
Some already had genes for resistance
The insecticide gave them resistance
They avoided the spray by choice
They grew resistant after being sprayed
A few mosquitoes already had resistance genes; they survived the spray and passed these genes on.
Why do doctors tell patients to finish all of their antibiotics?
To avoid leaving resistant bacteria alive
To make the bacteria grow faster
To help the bacteria become stronger
To make the medicine taste better
Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive, and they may multiply into a resistant population.
Rock pocket mice live on light sand and on dark lava rock. Which pattern would natural selection produce?
Dark mice on lava, light mice on sand
Light mice on lava, dark mice on sand
Only light mice in both places
Only dark mice in both places
In each habitat the mice that match their background are hidden from predators, so they survive and reproduce more.
A population of identical bacterial clones is exposed to an antibiotic, and none are resistant. What is most likely?
No resistance develops; they all die
All of them quickly become resistant
Half of them become resistant at once
They all learn to avoid the drug
Without variation there is no resistant individual to be selected, so resistance cannot spread.
Which observation shows that a trait is inherited?
Offspring share the trait with parents
The trait appears only after injury
The trait is learned in a classroom
The trait changes with each meal
When offspring share a trait with their parents, it is passed on through genes and can be acted on by natural selection.
Two populations of the same bird species live in different habitats for thousands of years. What might eventually happen?
They may become separate species
They will become identical copies
They will both stop reproducing
They will all migrate together
Different environments favour different traits, so isolated populations can change until they become separate species.
Arctic foxes have small ears and short legs. How does natural selection explain this?
Foxes that lost less heat survived better
Foxes shrank their ears to stay warm
Cold weather made each fox's ears smaller
Foxes chose shorter legs for snow
Small ears and short legs reduce heat loss, so foxes with these inherited traits survived and reproduced more in the cold.
Hunters often target elephants with large tusks. Over many years, what has happened in some populations?
More elephants are born without tusks
Elephants grow larger tusks than before
Elephants learn to hide their tusks
Tusk size stays exactly the same
Tuskless elephants were less likely to be hunted, so they survived and passed on this trait more often.
A fish population in a stream has both fast and slow swimmers. A fast predator is introduced. Predict what happens.
Fast swimmers become more common
Slow swimmers become more common
All fish become slow swimmers
The fish stop swimming entirely
Fast swimmers escape the predator more often, so they live to reproduce and pass on this trait.
Which statement correctly uses the idea of natural selection?
Helpful traits become common over generations
Animals change on purpose to fit in
All individuals in a group are identical
Traits change in a single lifetime
Natural selection makes helpful inherited traits more common in a population over many generations.
A disease kills most rabbits, but a few survive because of a gene. What happens to later generations?
More rabbits carry the protective gene
Fewer rabbits carry the protective gene
All rabbits lose the protective gene
No rabbit is ever born again
Survivors pass the protective gene to their offspring, so it becomes more common in the population.
Why do different species of Darwin's finches have different beak shapes on different islands?
Each island favoured beaks fit for its foods
Finches reshaped their beaks by pecking
Each finch picked a beak it liked
The islands all had identical foods
Different food sources on each island favoured different beak shapes, leading to different finch species.
Which piece of evidence would best support that natural selection changed a population?
Trait records over many generations
One photo of a single animal
A story about one animal's habits
The colour of one leaf in spring
Data on how common a trait is across many generations shows whether a population has changed.
Why is reproduction important for natural selection to change a population?
Traits pass on only through offspring
Reproduction makes animals stronger
Offspring choose their own traits
Reproduction stops all variation
Only traits passed to offspring can become more common, so survival alone is not enough without reproduction.
Walking-stick insects look like twigs. Which explanation is best?
Twig-like insects were eaten less often
Insects copied twigs by practising
Twigs turned some insects into sticks
Birds taught the insects to look odd
Insects that looked more like twigs were missed by predators, so they survived and passed on their shape.
sciXsFlCon: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
The anther, at the top of the stamen, produces pollen grains.
Which part of a flower catches pollen?
The sticky stigma at the top of the pistil traps pollen during pollination.
After fertilization, what does a flower's ovary develop into?
The ovary swells and ripens into the fruit, which surrounds and protects the seeds.
What does an ovule become after fertilization?
Each fertilized ovule develops into a seed containing a tiny plant.
Why do many flowers have bright petals and sweet nectar?
Colour and nectar attract insects and birds that carry pollen from flower to flower.
Conifer seeds are often described as "naked." What does this mean?
They are not enclosed in a fruit
They have no outer seed coat
Conifers are gymnosperms, meaning their seeds sit exposed on cone scales rather than inside a fruit.
Which of these plants is a conifer?
White spruce produces cones and needle-like leaves, so it is a conifer.
What is the first step in the life cycle of a seed plant once a seed lands in good soil?
Germination is when the seed sprouts and the young plant begins to grow.
What must happen before a flower can produce seeds?
The stem must lose its leaves
Pollination brings pollen to the stigma, which allows fertilization and seed development.
Male and female pine cones differ. Which describes male cones?
Male cones are small and soft and release large amounts of pollen into the wind.
Why do conifers produce huge amounts of pollen?
Wind pollination is a matter of chance
Insects need extra food to eat
Wind carries pollen randomly, so making lots of it increases the chance some reaches a female cone.
How do burrs, like burdock, spread their seeds?
By being blown by wind wings
Burrs have tiny hooks that catch on fur or clothing and are carried away.
Each dandelion seed has a fluffy parachute that lets the wind carry it far away.
How do animals help spread the seeds of fruits like blueberries?
They eat the fruit and drop the seeds
They plant the seeds on purpose
They carry pollen to the cones
They bury the leaves in soil
Animals eat the fruit and later pass the seeds in their droppings, often far from the parent plant.
Which is a key difference between flowering plants and conifers?
Both make seeds, but only flowering plants enclose their seeds in fruit.
Jack pine cones often stay closed until a certain event opens them. What is it?
The heat of a forest fire
Jack pine cones are sealed with resin that melts in the heat of a fire, releasing the seeds.
What is the young plant inside a seed called?
The embryo is the tiny undeveloped plant inside a seed.
What is the job of a seed's stored food?
To feed the young plant as it sprouts
To attract pollinators to the seed
To make the seed heavier for wind
To help the seed make pollen
The stored food gives the embryo energy until it can make its own food by photosynthesis.
Which is the correct order in the life cycle of a flowering plant?
A seed grows into a seedling, which matures and flowers, then forms fruit containing new seeds.
Which is the correct order in the life cycle of a pine tree?
A pine seed grows into a seedling and then a mature tree, which produces cones that hold new seeds.
What happens to a flower's petals after pollination and fertilization?
They usually wilt and fall off
Once fertilized, the flower no longer needs to attract pollinators, so the petals often wither while the fruit develops.
Maple trees produce winged seeds called samaras. How do these seeds travel?
Samaras have wings that make them spin like helicopters, letting the wind carry them away from the tree.
sciXsMossFern: Which is true about mosses?
They have no true roots, stems or leaves
They grow taller than most trees
They produce seeds inside fruit
They make pollen in small cones
Mosses are non-vascular plants that lack true roots, stems and leaves.
What tiny root-like threads hold a moss in place?
Rhizoids
Fronds
Cones
Petals
Rhizoids anchor mosses to soil or rock but do not carry water like real roots.
How do mosses take in water?
Directly through their surfaces
Through deep woody roots
Through tubes in a thick trunk
Through flowers and fruit
Lacking vascular tissue, mosses absorb water directly through their thin leaf-like parts.
What is the large leaf of a fern called?
A frond
A needle
A capsule
A petal
A fern's leaves are called fronds, and they often unroll from fiddleheads.
Where does a fern's underground stem grow?
Below the soil as a rhizome
High in the air as a trunk
Inside the spore capsule
On the tips of its fronds
Most ferns have an underground stem called a rhizome from which fronds and roots grow.
Which of these plants reproduces with spores, not seeds?
Sphagnum moss
Sugar maple
White pine
Wild rose
Sphagnum is a moss, and mosses reproduce with spores rather than seeds.
How is a spore different from a seed?
A spore has no stored food or embryo
A spore is much larger than a seed
A spore grows only inside fruit
A spore is made only in cones
A spore is a single cell without an embryo or food supply, while a seed contains both.
Ferns and mosses have two stages in their life cycle. What is this called?
Alternation of generations
Complete metamorphosis
Seed dispersal
Cross-pollination
Their life cycle switches between a spore-making stage and a sex-cell-making stage, called alternation of generations.
In a fern, which stage is the large, leafy plant we usually see?
The spore-producing stage
The heart-shaped stage
The egg-producing stage
The seed-producing stage
The familiar leafy fern is the sporophyte, the stage that makes spores.
In a moss, which stage is the green, leafy carpet we usually see?
The egg- and sperm-producing stage
The seed-producing stage
The pollen-producing stage
The fruit-producing stage
The green moss plant is the gametophyte, which makes eggs and sperm.
What grows from a fertilized egg on a fern prothallus?
A new leafy fern plant
A new spore capsule
A flower and fruit
A pine cone
The fertilized egg develops into the young leafy fern, which grows out of the prothallus.
What grows from a fertilized egg on a moss plant?
A stalk with a spore capsule
A new set of fronds
A small woody tree
A flower with petals
In mosses, the fertilized egg grows into a stalk topped with a capsule that makes spores.
What does a moss spore grow into when it lands in a damp spot?
A new green moss plant
A tall fern frond
A seed with a coat
A heart-shaped cone
A moss spore germinates into a thread-like growth that develops into a new green moss plant.
Why are mosses often called pioneer plants?
They can grow on bare rock first
They only grow in pine forests
They grow after all other plants
They need deep, rich soil
Mosses can colonize bare rock and help build soil that other plants later use.
Why can ferns grow taller than mosses?
Their vascular tissue moves water upward
They take in water through their spores
They have no need for any water
They store water in their fiddleheads
Vascular tissue carries water and nutrients up the plant, letting ferns grow larger.
What do the brown dots under a fern frond contain?
Spore cases full of spores
Seeds wrapped in fruit
Pollen for the wind
Stored drops of water
The brown dots are sori, clusters of spore cases that release spores.
How are fern spores released?
Spore cases dry and burst open
Bees carry them from flowers
Animals eat and drop them
They fall from ripe cones
When spore cases dry out they split open and fling spores into the air.
Which group of plants includes both mosses and ferns?
Seedless plants
Flowering plants
Conifers
Fruit trees
Mosses and ferns are seedless plants because they reproduce by spores.
Which habitat best suits most mosses?
A shady, damp forest floor
A dry, sunny desert dune
A salty, windy beach
A hot, rocky volcano top
Mosses need moisture for water uptake and for sperm to swim, so damp, shady places suit them.
A fern prothallus makes which of the following?
Eggs and sperm
Seeds and fruit
Pollen and cones
Flowers and nectar
The small heart-shaped prothallus produces eggs and sperm for sexual reproduction.
Fiddleheads of the ostrich fern are eaten in New Brunswick. What part of the fern are they?
Young fronds that are tightly curled
Seeds that grow inside fruit
Roots that grow below the soil
Spore cases that hang from stems
Fiddleheads are young, coiled fronds that unroll as the fern grows.
Peat moss is used by gardeners. Which property makes it useful in soil?
It holds a lot of water
It makes soil very dry
It adds sharp sand to soil
It produces many new seeds
Sphagnum peat moss soaks up and holds water, helping keep soil moist.
sciPhotoE: What liquid do plants take in through their roots for photosynthesis?
Plants absorb water through their roots and use it in photosynthesis.
Plants use light to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Through which tiny openings do leaves take in carbon dioxide?
Stomata are small pores, mostly on the underside of leaves, that let gases in and out.
Which part of most plants does the most photosynthesis?
Leaves are broad and full of chloroplasts, so they capture the most light.
Where is the energy from sunlight stored after photosynthesis?
Light energy is changed into chemical energy stored in glucose molecules.
How do plants release the energy stored in glucose?
Cellular respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to release usable energy.
Which process happens in plant cells both day and night?
Photosynthesis needs light, but cells respire all the time to get energy.
What do plants use some of their glucose to build?
Plants link glucose into cellulose, which forms strong cell walls.
How do plants store extra glucose for later?
Plants join glucose molecules into starch, which they store in roots, seeds and stems.
Leaves are full of green water
Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green.
What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when a plant is moved into darkness?
Photosynthesis needs light energy, so without light it cannot happen.
Which energy change happens when an animal eats a plant?
Chemical energy passes to the animal
Light energy passes to the animal
Sound energy passes to the animal
Nuclear energy passes to the animal
The chemical energy stored in the plant's food is transferred to the animal that eats it.
Plants produce their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers.
Where did the oxygen in the air we breathe mostly come from?
Photosynthesis by plants, algae and cyanobacteria released most of Earth's atmospheric oxygen.
Which tissue carries water from roots up to the leaves?
Xylem tubes carry water and minerals from the roots to the leaves.
Which tissue carries sugars made in the leaves to other parts of the plant?
Phloem tubes move sugars from the leaves to roots, stems, fruits and seeds.
A student puts a pondweed under a bright lamp and sees bubbles. What gas is in the bubbles?
Pondweed releases oxygen during photosynthesis, which forms bubbles in the water.
If the lamp is moved closer to the pondweed, what most likely happens to the bubbles?
More light increases the rate of photosynthesis, so more oxygen bubbles are released.
Why do maple leaves turn red and yellow in fall?
Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing other pigments
Leaves fill up with extra chlorophyll
Cold air paints the leaves new colours
Sunlight gets brighter in the fall
As days shorten, chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow and red pigments become visible.
Which of these is NOT needed for photosynthesis?
Photosynthesis uses light, water and carbon dioxide; nitrogen gas is not a raw material.
What type of energy do the products of photosynthesis store?
Glucose stores energy in its chemical bonds, which is chemical potential energy.
Which organisms depend on photosynthesis for their food energy?
Almost all food chains begin with producers, so nearly all organisms rely on photosynthesis.
sciXsPhoto: Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
A sunflower is a green plant with chloroplasts, so it makes its own food by photosynthesis.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Giant kelp is a large brown alga that uses sunlight to make food.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Duckweed is a tiny floating plant that photosynthesizes on the surface of ponds.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Black spruce is a conifer with green needles that carry out photosynthesis.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Diatoms are single-celled algae that photosynthesize and produce much of the ocean's oxygen.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Mosses are green plants with chloroplasts, so they photosynthesize.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Grass is a green plant that makes food from light, carbon dioxide and water.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
A cactus's green stem contains chlorophyll and carries out photosynthesis.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Ferns are green plants that photosynthesize in their fronds.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Sea lettuce is a green alga that makes its own food using sunlight.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
The corn plant has green leaves full of chloroplasts and makes its own food.
Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?
Water lilies are flowering plants whose floating leaves photosynthesize.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
A honey bee is an animal; it eats nectar and pollen instead of making its own food.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
Mushrooms are fungi; they absorb food from their surroundings and have no chlorophyll.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
Yeast is a fungus that feeds on sugars and cannot make its own food.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
A beluga is an animal that eats fish and other prey for energy.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
Ghost pipe is a white plant with no chlorophyll; it gets food from fungi in the soil.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
Penicillium is a fungus that absorbs food and has no chlorophyll.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
A tapeworm is a parasite that absorbs food from its host.
Which of these organisms does NOT carry out photosynthesis?
A monarch butterfly is an insect, so it must eat food rather than make it.
Which group of organisms contains only photosynthetic ones?
Roses, kelp and moss all contain chlorophyll and make their own food.
Which group of organisms contains only non-photosynthetic ones?
Wolves and beetles are animals and mushrooms are fungi, so none of them photosynthesize.
sciPopEco: Which level of organization is this? All the beavers living along one river.
A population is all the members of one species living in the same area.
Which level of organization is this? One single snowshoe hare.
One individual living thing is an organism, the simplest of these levels.
Which level of organization is this? All the plants, animals, fungi and bacteria living in a bog.
A community is all the populations of different species living together in one area.
Which level of organization is this? A boreal forest with its trees, animals, soil, water and climate.
An ecosystem includes the living community plus the non-living parts of the environment.
Which level of organization is this? All the sugar maples in a woodlot.
All the sugar maples are one species in one place, so they form a population.
Which level of organization is this? The caribou, wolves, lichens and birds sharing a stretch of tundra.
Several species living together without counting non-living parts make a community.
Which level of organization is this? A tidal pool with its seaweed, snails, salt water and rocks.
The tidal pool includes both living things and non-living things like water and rocks, so it is an ecosystem.
Which level of organization is this? A single bald eagle nesting by a lake.
One individual eagle is an organism.
Which level of organization is this? All the monarch butterflies in a meadow.
A group of the same species in one area is a population.
Which level of organization is this? A city park: its trees, birds, squirrels, soil, pond and sunlight.
The park includes living things and non-living factors, so it is an ecosystem.
Which level of organization is this? All the different fish species in Lake Erie.
Several different species living together form a community (here, a fish community).
Which level of organization is this? All the walleye in Lake Erie.
All the walleye are one species in one lake, so they form a population.
What is the difference between a community and an ecosystem?
An ecosystem also includes non-living things
A community also includes non-living things
An ecosystem has only one species
A community has only one organism
A community is only the living things; an ecosystem adds non-living factors like water, soil and air.
What is the difference between a population and a community?
A community has many different species
A population has many different species
A community has only one species
A population includes the soil and water
A population is one species, while a community includes all the different species in an area.
Which is a non-living (abiotic) part of an ecosystem?
Sunlight is not alive, so it is an abiotic factor in an ecosystem.
Which is a living (biotic) part of an ecosystem?
Fungi are living organisms, so they are a biotic factor.
Which list is in order from smallest to largest level?
One organism belongs to a population, populations form a community, and a community plus its surroundings makes an ecosystem.
Which level of organization is the largest of these?
An ecosystem contains communities, which contain populations, which contain organisms.
A scientist counts all the loons on one lake. What is she studying?
Counting one species in one area means studying a population.
A scientist studies how rainfall and soil affect all the species in a wetland. What is she studying?
Studying living things together with non-living factors like rain and soil means studying an ecosystem.
Which level of organization is this? All the people living in Halifax.
All the humans in one city are one species in one area, which is a population.
Which level of organization is this? All the bees, flowers, birds and worms in a garden.
Many different species living together in an area make a community.
sciORG: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane, while animal cells do not.
Which organelle captures light energy to make sugar?
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which captures light energy for photosynthesis.
What green pigment is found inside chloroplasts?
Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light.
Which organelle is usually much larger in plant cells than in animal cells?
Plant cells often have one large central vacuole that stores water and helps keep the cell firm.
Which structure is found in BOTH plant and animal cells?
Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria to release energy from food.
What is the main job of the nucleus?
To store large amounts of water
To give the cell a stiff shape
The nucleus holds the cell's DNA and directs the cell's activities.
What does a cell's DNA contain?
DNA carries the genetic instructions that tell the cell how to grow and work.
Which organelle packages and ships proteins to other parts of the cell?
The Golgi apparatus sorts, packages and sends proteins where they are needed.
Which organelle is a network of membranes that moves materials through the cell?
The endoplasmic reticulum is a system of folded membranes that transports materials inside the cell.
Which organelle contains chemicals that break down waste and old cell parts?
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste, worn-out parts and invaders.
Ribosomes can be attached to which organelle, giving it a bumpy look?
Rough ER is covered with ribosomes, which make proteins.
In which organelle does cellular respiration take place?
Mitochondria break down sugar with oxygen to release energy for the cell.
Which structure in a plant cell is made mostly of cellulose?
The plant cell wall is built from cellulose fibres, which make it strong.
Which part of the cell is described as "selectively permeable"?
The cell membrane lets some substances in and out while keeping others out.
A wilted plant has cells that have lost water. Which organelle has shrunk?
When the central vacuole loses water, plant cells lose firmness and the plant wilts.
Which organelle would you NOT find in a human skin cell?
Animal cells do not photosynthesize, so they have no chloroplasts.
Which cell part would you NOT find in a bacterium?
Bacteria are prokaryotes, so their DNA floats in the cytoplasm without a nucleus.
Which structure inside the nucleus helps make ribosomes?
The nucleolus is a dense region of the nucleus where ribosome parts are made.
Why do muscle cells contain many mitochondria?
They need a lot of energy
Muscles use a lot of energy, so they need many mitochondria to release it.
Why do leaf cells have more chloroplasts than root cells?
Roots need more energy than leaves
Leaves receive light, so their cells hold many chloroplasts to make food; roots are underground in the dark.
Which organelle is like a factory's manager's office, holding the plans?
Like an office holding plans, the nucleus holds DNA, the instructions for the cell.
Which organelle is like a storage warehouse?
Vacuoles store water, food and wastes, much like a warehouse stores supplies.
sciXsCoral: Coral polyps get most of their food from algae living inside them. What are these algae called?
Zooxanthellae
Plankton nets
Sea anemones
Sponges
Tiny algae called zooxanthellae live in coral tissue and share sugars they make by photosynthesis.
What do corals give the algae living inside them?
Shelter and nutrients
Sunlight and fresh water
Shells and sand
Salt and ice
The coral provides a protected home and nutrients, while the algae provide food: a mutualism.
What happens to corals if they stay bleached for a long time?
They can starve and die
They grow stronger and larger
They turn into new algae
They swim to cooler water
Without their algae, corals lose their main food supply and may die if conditions do not improve.
What is the main cause of mass coral bleaching events?
Ocean water that is too warm
Ocean water that is too cold
Too many fish on the reef
Strong sunlight at night
Unusually warm water stresses corals so they expel their algae.
What is the largest coral reef system in the world?
The Great Barrier Reef
The Grand Banks
The Bay of Fundy
The Mariana Trench
The Great Barrier Reef off northeastern Australia is the world's largest reef system.
How does ocean acidification harm corals?
It makes building skeletons harder
It makes the water much colder
It adds extra sunlight to reefs
It gives corals more algae
More acidic water has less carbonate available, so corals struggle to build their calcium carbonate skeletons.
What causes ocean acidification?
The ocean absorbing extra carbon dioxide
The ocean absorbing extra oxygen
Too much salt washing off land
Fish releasing acids in water
When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater it forms carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH.
Some medicines have been developed from chemicals found in reef animals. Why does this matter?
Reefs may hold future medicines
Reefs make all medicines today
Medicines grow coral faster
Reefs remove all diseases
Reef species produce unusual chemicals that scientists study for new medicines, so losing reefs could mean losing discoveries.
How does overfishing of plant-eating fish harm a reef?
Seaweed overgrows the coral
Coral grows too quickly
The water becomes too cold
Sharks eat all the coral
Plant-eating fish keep seaweed in check; without them, seaweed can smother corals.
Why is using dynamite or poison to catch fish harmful to reefs?
It destroys coral and kills many species
It helps coral polyps grow faster
It makes the water clearer for algae
It only affects the fish being caught
Blast and poison fishing kill corals and many non-target animals, damaging the whole reef.
How can tourists help protect coral reefs?
Avoid touching or standing on coral
Break off coral as a souvenir
Feed fish leftover snacks
Anchor boats on the reef
Coral polyps are fragile, so touching or stepping on them can injure or kill them.
What is a marine protected area?
A part of the ocean with limits on harmful use
A beach where only swimming is allowed
A fish farm built on top of a reef
A zone where boats can dump waste
Marine protected areas restrict activities like fishing to let reefs and wildlife recover.
Why do sediments from cleared land harm reefs?
They cloud the water and block sunlight
They add sunlight to the water
They feed the coral polyps directly
They make the water much warmer
Mud washed off cleared land clouds the water so the algae inside corals cannot get enough light.
Which choice is a solution to reduce farm runoff reaching reefs?
Use less fertilizer and plant buffer strips
Spray more fertilizer near rivers
Clear riverbank trees and shrubs
Pump farm waste into the sea
Using less fertilizer and planting vegetation along streams traps nutrients before they reach the ocean.
Why is reducing carbon dioxide emissions important for coral reefs?
It limits ocean warming and acidification
It makes the ocean saltier for coral
It adds more algae blooms to reefs
It lowers sea levels quickly
Less carbon dioxide means less heating and less acidification, the two biggest global threats to reefs.
What do coral reefs provide for many young fish?
A sheltered nursery habitat
A cold, deep hiding spot
A source of fresh water
A floating ice platform
The many cracks and spaces in reefs shelter young fish from predators while they grow.
How do reefs help coastal economies?
They draw tourists and support fisheries
They produce oil for fuel
They provide wood for building
They grow crops for farming
Reefs attract divers and snorkellers and support fish that people catch and sell.
Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but are home to about what fraction of marine species?
About one quarter
About one thousandth
About nine tenths
About one millionth
Although small in area, reefs support roughly 25% of all known marine species.
Scientists are growing coral fragments in nurseries and replanting them. What is the goal?
To help restore damaged reefs
To sell coral for jewellery
To replace all wild coral
To make the water warmer
Coral gardening grows healthy corals and plants them on damaged reefs to speed recovery.
Which kind of coral builds large reefs?
Hard (stony) coral
Soft coral only
Jellyfish colonies
Sea sponges
Hard corals build calcium carbonate skeletons that pile up over time to form reefs.
Why are some sunscreens a concern for coral reefs?
Some chemicals in them may harm corals
They cool the ocean water too much
They give corals extra food
They make the water too clear
Studies suggest some sunscreen chemicals can damage coral, so reef-safe products are recommended.
Why do most coral reefs grow in tropical waters?
Reef corals need warm, clear water
Reef corals need icy, dark water
Reef corals need fresh river water
Reef corals need muddy water
Reef-building corals and their algae thrive in warm, clear, sunlit tropical seas.
sciXsGroundW: Where does groundwater come from?
Rain and snowmelt soaking into the ground
Water made deep inside rocks
Water pumped down from the ocean
Water released from tree roots
Precipitation seeps down through soil and fills spaces in rock and sediment, becoming groundwater.
What is the water table?
The top of the zone filled with groundwater
The bottom of a lake or river
A table used to measure rainfall
The surface of the ocean
Below the water table, all the spaces in the ground are filled with water.
What is groundwater recharge?
Water refilling an aquifer from the surface
Water pumped out by a well
Water evaporating from a lake
Water flowing out to sea
Recharge happens when rain and snowmelt soak down and add water to an aquifer.
Which type of ground lets water soak in most easily?
Sand and gravel
Clay
Pavement
Solid granite
Sand and gravel have large connected spaces, so water passes through them quickly.
Claim: Wetlands help recharge groundwater. Which evidence supports it?
Water levels in wells near wetlands stay higher
Wetlands are often home to many frogs
Wetlands look green during summer
Wetlands freeze over in winter
Higher well levels near wetlands show that water from the wetland soaks down into the ground.
Claim: A new factory is polluting the town's groundwater. Which evidence would best support it?
Wells near the factory show a chemical it uses
The factory has a very tall chimney
The factory hired many new workers
The factory is painted bright grey
Finding the factory's chemical in nearby well water directly links the pollution to the factory.
Claim: Groundwater supplies are always unlimited. Is this claim supported?
No — aquifers can run low if overpumped
Yes — groundwater refills instantly
Yes — rain falls every single day
No — groundwater does not exist
Water pumped faster than it recharges lowers aquifer levels, so supplies are not unlimited.
Which evidence would best show that an aquifer has recovered?
Well water levels rising over several years
A single rainy weekend in spring
More people moving to the town
A new well drilled nearby
A steady rise in water levels over years shows the aquifer is refilling.
Claim: Road salt can contaminate groundwater. Which evidence supports it?
Wells near busy roads have higher chloride levels
Roads are slippery in winter months
Salt melts snow on the sidewalk
Cars drive slower when roads are icy
Higher chloride in wells near salted roads shows salt is seeping into the groundwater.
Why are rain gardens good for groundwater?
They let rain soak into the soil
They send rain straight to sewers
They cover soil with pavement
They pump water out of wells
Rain gardens collect runoff and let it soak in, adding to groundwater recharge.
About what fraction of Canadians rely on groundwater for drinking water?
About one third
Almost none
Only city dwellers
Exactly everyone
Roughly 30% of Canadians, especially in rural areas, get their drinking water from groundwater.
Why can a polluted aquifer be hard to clean?
Water moves slowly through rock underground
Pollution floats away right away
Aquifers are easy to reach by hand
Sunlight breaks up the pollution
Groundwater moves slowly and is hidden underground, so pollutants can linger for years.
Claim: Watering lawns at midday wastes groundwater. Which reasoning supports it?
More water evaporates in the hot afternoon
Grass only drinks water at night
Midday water turns into salt water
Sunlight makes the water vanish underground
Watering in the heat of the day loses more water to evaporation, so more must be pumped.
Which is the strongest evidence that a well is drawing down a nearby stream?
Stream flow drops whenever the well pumps
The stream is home to many trout
The well is painted a bright colour
The stream freezes in the winter
If stream flow falls each time the well runs, it suggests the well is pulling water the stream would receive.
A town replaces flood irrigation with drip irrigation on its farms. What result would support the claim that this saves groundwater?
Less water is pumped for the same crops
Crops grow in a different colour
Farmers buy more tractors each year
It rains more often in the area
Using less pumped water while still growing the same crops shows groundwater is being saved.
Claim: Old abandoned wells can let pollution reach aquifers. Is this supported?
Yes — they give surface water a direct path down
No — old wells are full of solid rock
No — pollution cannot move downward
Yes — they add fresh rain to the ocean
An unsealed well acts like a pipe that lets contaminated surface water flow straight into the aquifer.
Which action would most reduce a household's groundwater use?
Fixing leaky taps and toilets
Leaving the hose running
Washing the car every day
Taking longer showers
Leaks can waste large amounts of water, so fixing them reduces the water pumped from wells.
Why do scientists use monitoring wells?
To measure groundwater levels and quality
To supply water to the whole city
To store rainwater for gardens
To catch fish living underground
Monitoring wells let scientists track how groundwater levels and pollution change over time.
Claim: Pesticides sprayed on fields can reach groundwater. Which evidence supports it?
Traces of the pesticide found in farm wells
The crops grew taller that year
Fewer insects ate the crops
The fields were sprayed in spring
Detecting the pesticide in well water shows it moved down through the soil into the groundwater.
What might happen to the land surface when large amounts of groundwater are removed?
It can slowly sink
It can rise into mountains
It can turn into sand dunes
It can become a glacier
Removing water lets underground sediments compact, so the land above can slowly sink.
Claim: Planting trees and grass increases groundwater recharge compared with bare, packed soil. Is this supported?
Yes — roots loosen soil so water soaks in
No — plants block all water from soil
No — bare soil absorbs the most rain
Yes — plants make water from sunlight
Plant roots and leaf litter loosen soil and slow runoff, helping water infiltrate.
Which source gives the most reliable evidence about a town's groundwater levels?
Years of measurements from local wells
One resident's opinion online
A guess based on a single storm
A photo of a dry flower bed
Long-term measured data is far more reliable than opinions or single observations.
